Diffusion between two bulbs

Step 1 / 5 Stage Hover a molecule for its identity and molar mass. Click a bulb, the stopcock, or a panel for an explanation.

plan.contextChunk: This figure contains three panels labeled (a), (b), and (c) that illustrate the process of gaseous diffusion as two initially separated gases mix after a connecting stopcock is opened. In panel (a), 'Stopcock closed,' all small white dots representing H2 molecules are confined to the left bulb and all red dots representing O2 molecules are densely packed in the right bulb, with the closed stopcock valve preventing any exchange. In panel (b), 'Stopcock open,' a small number of white H2 molecules have already dispersed into the O2-side bulb while fewer red O2 molecules have crossed to the H2 side, reflecting the faster diffusion rate of the lighter, less massive H2 gas. In panel (c), 'Some time after Stopcock open,' both white and red dots are distributed approximately uniformly across both bulbs, indicating that the concentration gradients have largely equalized through continued random molecular motion. This figure demonstrates that diffusion is driven by concentration gradients and that lighter gases diffuse more rapidly than heavier ones, motivating the quantitative relationship described by Graham's law of effusion.

interactionPlan.concept: When a stopcock connects two bulbs holding different gases, random molecular motion alone carries each gas down its own concentration gradient until the mixture is uniform — and the lighter H₂ spreads faster than the heavier O₂.
elements: Default triptych layout: three identical two-bulb apparatuses drawn small and side by side across the canvas, labeled (a), (b), (c)
Each apparatus: left spherical glass bulb and right spherical glass bulb, pale blue-green fill, blue-gray outline, soft upper-left highlight
Short horizontal connecting tube joining the bulbs, blending into each bulb through necked junctions (tube walls curve into the sphere outline, not a plain rounded rectangle butted against it)

Stopcock assembly on the tube: slim vertical stem rising from a narrow collar on the tube, barrel body, and a flared handle wheel (wide splayed knob plate) on top; a short slim lower stem below the bore
Valve plug state: a vertical bar blocking the bore when closed, clear bore when open
White circular dots with faint gray edge = H₂ molecules (~30 in the left bulb at t=0)
Bright red circular dots = O₂ molecules (~32 in the right bulb at t=0)
'H₂' label above the left bulb and 'O₂' above the right bulb of panel (a)
Caption under each panel: 'Stopcock closed', 'Stopcock open', 'Some time after stopcock opened'
Panel letter (a), (b), (c) on a line beneath each caption
Single-panel drill-down view: one large apparatus centered, same styling, with large per-bulb counters reading 'H₂: 30   O₂: 0' in ~14px dark gray (hidden in the triptych view)
Mass-coded overlay (optional view): long faint motion trails on H₂ dots, short trails on O₂ dots
Mass legend for the mass-coded view: 'H₂ = 2 g/mol — fast' and 'O₂ = 32 g/mol — slow'

interactions.teaches: The textbook's three panels are three frozen moments of one continuous process; switching to the single enlarged apparatus lets the learner run that process themselves.
interactions.label: View

interactions.teaches: Sealed gradient, early asymmetric mixing, and final uniform distribution are the three qualitative regimes of diffusion.
interactions.label: Panel

interactions.teaches: Diffusion is continuous, not three snapshots: advancing time smoothly shrinks each gas's concentration gradient until both bulbs hold the same mixture, with net transfer slowing as the gradient fades.
interactions.label: Elapsed time after opening (arbitrary units)

interactions.teaches: Mixing is driven by aimless random motion — every molecule wanders both ways, and net flow exists only because more molecules start on one side.
interactions.label: Play diffusion

interactions.teaches: At the same temperature lighter molecules move faster, so H₂ invades the O₂ bulb sooner and in greater numbers than O₂ crosses back — the seed of Graham's law.
interactions.label: Molecular-mass view

demo_steps.title: The textbook figure
demo_steps.narration: Three snapshots of the same apparatus: (a) the stopcock is closed with H₂ sealed left and O₂ sealed right, (b) the valve has just been opened and molecules begin crossing, (c) long afterward both bulbs hold the same mixture.

demo_steps.title: Zoom into one apparatus
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the single enlarged apparatus, still sealed. Counters appear under each bulb: H₂: 30, O₂: 0 on the left and H₂: 0, O₂: 32 on the right — a maximum gradient with nowhere to go.

demo_steps.title: Open the valve
demo_steps.narration: Turn the stopcock handle and the bore clears. Molecules wander across in both directions, but the counters already show an asymmetry: more white H₂ dots have reached the right bulb than red O₂ dots have reached the left.

demo_steps.title: Why H₂ leads
demo_steps.narration: In the mass-coded view, H₂ at 2 g/mol carries long fast trails and O₂ at 32 g/mol short slow ones. Same temperature, same average kinetic energy — so the lighter gas moves about four times faster and spreads correspondingly sooner.

demo_steps.title: Uniform mixture
demo_steps.narration: Push time to the end: both bulbs show the same salt-and-pepper blend and the counters match. Molecules still cross the stopcock constantly, now equally in both directions — equilibrium is balance, not stillness.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Diffusion needs no pump — random motion alone erases a concentration gradient, and because lighter molecules move faster at the same temperature, H₂ invades the O₂ bulb faster than O₂ invades the H₂ bulb.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: STEP-0 DEFAULT must reproduce the textbook composition: three small two-bulb apparatuses in a horizontal row across a wide canvas, panel (a) left, (b) center, (c) right, with a plain dark-gray caption and panel letter centered under each. In this triptych view show NO counters, NO legend, and NO divider line — just glassware and dots, matching the clean source. Only panel (a) carries the 'H₂' and 'O₂' bulb labels. Glassware: two equal pale blue-green spheres with blue-gray outlines and a soft light highlight in the upper-left, joined at their equators by a short tube whose walls neck smoothly into each sphere (draw the junction as a concave fillet, never a rectangle abutting a circle). The stopcock sits mid-tube: a narrow collar on the tube, a slim vertical stem, a small barrel around the bore, and a wide flared handle wheel on top, plus a short slim stem below — all in the same blue-gray line weight. Closed state shows a vertical plug bar across the bore; open state shows the bore clear and the handle rotated a quarter turn. Never draw a dashed vertical divider anywhere. Molecules are small filled circles: H₂ pure white with a faint gray edge, O₂ bright red, scattered randomly inside the sphere interiors without overlap. Panel (a): ~30 white left, ~32 red right, none in the tube. Panel (b): a handful of white dots already in the right bulb, noticeably fewer red dots in the left. Panel (c): an even mix of both colors in both bulbs. SINGLE-PANEL VIEW: one large apparatus centered, same styling, with a legible ~14px dark-gray counter block beneath each bulb reading 'H₂: 30   O₂: 0' style totals that update live, plus (in mass-coded mode) faint long trails behind H₂ dots, short trails behind O₂ dots, and a small corner legend 'H₂ 2 g/mol — fast' / 'O₂ 32 g/mol — slow'. Palette limited to pale teal glass, blue-gray outlines, white, red, and dark-gray text.

authoredContext:
In general, we know that when a sample of gas is introduced to one part of a closed container, its molecules very quickly disperse throughout the container; this process by which molecules disperse in space in response to differences in concentration is called diffusion (shown in ). The gaseous atoms or molecules are, of course, unaware of any concentration gradient, they simply move randomly—regions of higher concentration have more particles than regions of lower concentrations, and so a net movement of species from high to low concentration areas takes place. In a closed environment, diffusion will ultimately result in equal concentrations of gas throughout, as depicted in . The gaseous atoms and molecules continue to move, but since their concentrations are the same in both bulbs, the rates of transfer between the bulbs are equal (no net transfer of molecules occurs).

Explain why the numbers of molecules are not identical in the left- and right-hand bulbs shown in the center illustration of .

(a) Two gases, H 2 and O 2 , are initially separated. (b) When the stopcock is opened, they mix together. The lighter gas, H 2 , passes through the opening faster than O 2 , so just after the stopcock is opened, more H 2 molecules move to the O 2 side than O 2 molecules move to the H 2 side. (c) After a short time, both the slower-moving O 2 molecules and the faster-moving H 2 molecules have distributed themselves evenly on both sides of the vessel.

In this figure, three pairs of gas filled spheres or vessels are shown connected with a stopcock between them. In a, the figure is labeled, “Stopcock closed.” Above, the left sphere is labeled, “H subscript 2.” It contains approximately 30 small, white, evenly distributed circles. The sphere to its right is labeled, “O subscript 2.” It contains approximately 30 small red evenly distributed circles. In b, the figure is labeled, “Stopcock open.” The stopcock valve handle is now parallel to the tube connecting the two spheres. On the left, approximately 9 small, white circles and 4 small, red circles are present, with the red spheres appearing slightly closer to the stopcock. On the right side, approximately 25 small, red spheres and 21 small, white spheres are present, with the concentration of white spheres slightly greater near the stopcock. In c, the figure is labeled “Some time after Stopcock open.” In this situation, the red and white spheres appear evenly mixed and uniformly distributed throughout both spheres.

demo_steps.title: Two gases, one barrier
demo_steps.narration: The stopcock is closed: every white H2 molecule is trapped in the left bulb and every red O2 molecule in the right. Each gas sits on a maximum concentration gradient with nowhere to go.

demo_steps.title: Open the valve
demo_steps.narration: With the bore clear, molecules begin wandering across. Notice the asymmetry: several white dots have already reached the right bulb while only a few red dots have made it left.

demo_steps.title: Why H2 leads
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the mass-coded view: H2 at 2 g/mol carries long fast trails, O2 at 32 g/mol short slow ones. At the same temperature the lighter gas has the higher average speed, so it spreads roughly four times faster.

demo_steps.title: Sweep time forward
demo_steps.narration: Drag the time slider and watch the counters: net transfer slows as each gradient shrinks, even though individual molecules never stop moving.

demo_steps.title: Uniform mixture
demo_steps.narration: Long after opening, both bulbs contain the same blend of white and red. Molecules still cross the stopcock constantly, but now equally in both directions — equilibrium, not stillness.

plan.keyInsight: Diffusion needs no pump — random motion alone erases a concentration gradient, and because lighter molecules move faster at the same temperature, H2 invades the O2 bulb faster than O2 invades the H2 bulb.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Single horizontal apparatus centered in a wide canvas: two equal pale blue-green spheres with a blue-gray outline and a soft light highlight in the upper-left of each, joined at their equators by a short tube carrying a schematic stopcock (barrel, oval handle plate on top, small stem below) drawn in the same blue-gray. Above the left bulb the label 'H2', above the right 'O2', with proper subscripts. Molecules are small filled circles: H2 pure white with a faint gray edge, O2 bright red. At time 0 the left bulb holds ~30 white dots scattered at random and the right bulb ~32 red dots, both filling their spheres evenly with no overlap and none inside the tube. As time advances, dots migrate across the tube; at intermediate time the right bulb should visibly contain more white intruders than the left contains red ones. At full time both bulbs show an even salt-and-pepper mix of roughly equal counts. Caption text sits centered below the apparatus in plain dark gray, with the panel letter on a second line. In mass-coded mode, give each H2 dot a long faint motion trail and each O2 dot a short one, and show a small legend reading 'H2 2 g/mol — fast' and 'O2 32 g/mol — slow'. Add a small live counter under each bulb listing white and red totals, and a faint dashed vertical divider at the stopcock. Hovering a dot pops a small tooltip naming the molecule and its molar mass. Keep the palette limited to the pale teal glass, blue-gray outlines, white, and red so the two gases read instantly.

discrepancies: The source is a three-panel triptych (a)(b)(c) shown side-by-side; the generated figure shows only one panel at a time. A stage toggle exists, so this is defensible, but the at-a-glance side-by-side comparison of closed/open/mixed that the original conveys is lost.

Added elements not in the source: a dashed vertical divider line through the stopcock extending above and below the apparatus, and per-bulb molecule counters (white dot 30 / red dot 0) beneath each bulb.

The stopcock rendering is simplified relative to the source's detailed valve (source has a distinct upper handle wheel, barrel with visible plug and a lower stem/collar); the generated version reads as stacked rectangles/ellipses and the lower stem is thinner and shorter than in the source.
The counter numerals and their dot keys under each bulb are noticeably smaller than any text in the source and sit in whitespace the source leaves empty, cluttering the caption zone.

Bulb-to-tube junction in the source has a flared/necked connection blending into the spheres; here the tube is a plain rounded rectangle overlapping the circles, so the glassware silhouette is slightly cruder.
evaluation.notes: A well-executed, chemically accurate reproduction of the two-bulb diffusion figure with a rich set of genuinely pedagogical controls (stage toggles, time slider, play animation, mass-trail view, 5-step narration); main weaknesses are the loss of the source's side-by-side triptych composition and added non-source chrome (dashed divider, tiny molecule counters) that clutters the caption area.

Enlarge and relabel the per-bulb counters (e.g. 'H₂: 30  O₂: 0' at ~13–14px) or hide them in the default (a) state so the step-0 view matches the clean source image.

Refine the stopcock geometry: add the flared handle wheel and slimmer lower stem/collar seen in the source, and blend the tube ends into the bulbs with necked junctions rather than a plain rounded rectangle.
Consider a 'show all three panels' option that renders (a), (b), (c) as three small apparatuses in a row, matching the source's default composition.

Diffusion between two bulbs

Step 1 / 5 Stage Hover a molecule for its identity and molar mass. Click a bulb, the stopcock, or a panel for an explanation.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: Molecule distribution inside the bulbs differs in texture: in the source the dots fill each bulb fairly uniformly, while in the generated panel (c) (and the right bulb of (b)) the dots cluster toward the periphery leaving a visibly empty centre, making the 'uniform mixture' message less convincing.

The default triptych is drawn into a 1320×400 viewBox inside a much taller container, so the whole apparatus renders small with a lot of vertical whitespace; captions ('Stopcock closed', '(a)') and the H₂/O₂ labels end up noticeably smaller than in the source, where they are prominent.

The stopcock assembly is simplified: the source valve has a clearly visible barrel with a dark inner plug and a distinctly wider top wheel/handle; the generated valve reads as a small stack of pale rectangles and is less recognisable as a stopcock at this scale.

Source panel (c) shows both bulbs containing a comparable red/white blend; in the generated (c) the right bulb still looks red-dominant with relatively few white dots, weakening the 'same mixture on both sides' point.

Extra chrome not in the source (per-bulb molecule counters, mass legend, panel hit-boxes) exists in the single-apparatus view — acceptable as UI, but the counters sit close to the caption block and could crowd it.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-coloured reproduction of the three-panel two-bulb diffusion figure with an unusually rich and pedagogically apt interaction set (stage buttons, time slider, play animation, mass/speed-trail mode, stepped narration); main weaknesses are the undersized default rendering with small captions and slightly ring-like, non-uniform molecule distributions in panels (b)/(c).

feedback.rationale: Concept and interaction structure are correct (concept 5, no failure modes or action items), but execution details — undersized viewBox with small captions, ring-like molecule distributions, and a simplified stopcock — need concrete rendering fixes.

interactions.label: View

interactions.teaches: Sealed gradient, early asymmetric mixing, and final uniform distribution are the three qualitative regimes of diffusion.
interactions.label: Panel

interactions.teaches: Diffusion is continuous, not three snapshots: advancing time smoothly shrinks each gas's concentration gradient until both bulbs hold the same mixture, with net transfer slowing as the gradient fades.
interactions.label: Elapsed time after opening (arbitrary units)

interactions.teaches: Mixing is driven by aimless random motion — every molecule wanders both ways, and net flow exists only because more molecules start on one side.
interactions.label: Play diffusion

interactions.teaches: At the same temperature lighter molecules move faster, so H₂ invades the O₂ bulb sooner and in greater numbers than O₂ crosses back — the seed of Graham's law.
interactions.label: Molecular-mass view

demo_steps.title: The textbook figure
demo_steps.narration: Three snapshots of the same apparatus: (a) the stopcock is closed with H₂ sealed left and O₂ sealed right, (b) the valve has just been opened and molecules begin crossing, (c) long afterward both bulbs hold the same mixture.

demo_steps.title: Zoom into one apparatus
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the single enlarged apparatus, still sealed. Counters appear under each bulb: H₂: 30, O₂: 0 on the left and H₂: 0, O₂: 32 on the right — a maximum gradient with nowhere to go.

demo_steps.title: Open the valve
demo_steps.narration: Turn the stopcock handle and the bore clears. Molecules wander across in both directions, but the counters already show an asymmetry: more white H₂ dots have reached the right bulb than red O₂ dots have reached the left.

demo_steps.title: Why H₂ leads
demo_steps.narration: In the mass-coded view, H₂ at 2 g/mol carries long fast trails and O₂ at 32 g/mol short slow ones. Same temperature, same average kinetic energy — so the lighter gas moves about four times faster and spreads correspondingly sooner.

demo_steps.title: Uniform mixture
demo_steps.narration: Push time to the end: both bulbs show the same salt-and-pepper blend and the counters match. Molecules still cross the stopcock constantly, now equally in both directions — equilibrium is balance, not stillness.

plan.keyInsight: Diffusion needs no pump — random motion alone erases a concentration gradient, and because lighter molecules move faster at the same temperature, H₂ invades the O₂ bulb faster than O₂ invades the H₂ bulb.
plan.reconstructionNotes: STEP-0 DEFAULT must reproduce the textbook composition: three small two-bulb apparatuses in a horizontal row across a wide canvas, panel (a) left, (b) center, (c) right, with a plain dark-gray caption and panel letter centered under each. In this triptych view show NO counters, NO legend, and NO divider line — just glassware and dots, matching the clean source. Only panel (a) carries the 'H₂' and 'O₂' bulb labels. Glassware: two equal pale blue-green spheres with blue-gray outlines and a soft light highlight in the upper-left, joined at their equators by a short tube whose walls neck smoothly into each sphere (draw the junction as a concave fillet, never a rectangle abutting a circle). The stopcock sits mid-tube: a narrow collar on the tube, a slim vertical stem, a small barrel around the bore, and a wide flared handle wheel on top, plus a short slim stem below — all in the same blue-gray line weight. Closed state shows a vertical plug bar across the bore; open state shows the bore clear and the handle rotated a quarter turn. Never draw a dashed vertical divider anywhere. Molecules are small filled circles: H₂ pure white with a faint gray edge, O₂ bright red, scattered randomly inside the sphere interiors without overlap. Panel (a): ~30 white left, ~32 red right, none in the tube. Panel (b): a handful of white dots already in the right bulb, noticeably fewer red dots in the left. Panel (c): an even mix of both colors in both bulbs. SINGLE-PANEL VIEW: one large apparatus centered, same styling, with a legible ~14px dark-gray counter block beneath each bulb reading 'H₂: 30   O₂: 0' style totals that update live, plus (in mass-coded mode) faint long trails behind H₂ dots, short trails behind O₂ dots, and a small corner legend 'H₂ 2 g/mol — fast' / 'O₂ 32 g/mol — slow'. Palette limited to pale teal glass, blue-gray outlines, white, red, and dark-gray text.

discrepancies: Overall scale/composition: the triptych is drawn in a 1240×350 viewBox letterboxed into a tall container, so the apparatus renders quite small with large empty bands above and below; in the source the three bulb pairs fill the frame and the dots read clearly.

Molecule distribution inside the bulbs is less uniform than the source — in panel (a) the red O₂ dots look clustered toward the bulb centre with a visible empty rim, whereas the source spreads dots evenly out to near the glass wall; dot radius relative to bulb radius also reads smaller than the source.

Panel (c) in the generated figure appears to contain noticeably fewer visible dots per bulb than panels (a)/(b) (molecules overlapping near the tube/centre), while the source shows a comparable total dot density in all three panels.

The stopcock handle in panel (b)/(c) is horizontally squashed (scale(0.42,1)) to indicate 'open'; the source draws the identical valve glyph in all three panels, so the open panels look slightly different in hardware rather than just in state.
Caption/label type is small at inline size relative to the source, where 'Stopcock closed', '(a)' etc. are prominent; the H₂/O₂ labels sit close to the bulb outline.
evaluation.notes: A recognizable and well-built reproduction of the three-panel two-bulb diffusion figure with correct glassware, stopcock, white-H₂/red-O₂ coding and matching captions, backed by a rich and genuinely pedagogical set of interactions (step player, stage buttons, time slider, play animation, mass/trail view, tooltips and popups); the main weaknesses are the shrunken letterboxed layout, slightly clustered/undersized molecule distributions, and somewhat small caption type.
action_items: Enlarge the default triptych: use a viewBox aspect closer to the container (or increase the apparatus scale/reduce vertical padding) so the bulbs and dots read at source size instead of being letterboxed in a tall frame.

Tune discSlots (reduce the boundary-distance weighting and/or increase dot radius) so molecules fill each bulb evenly out toward the rim, matching the source's uniform speckle, and verify panel (c) shows the same total dot count as (a) and (b).
Increase caption and H₂/O₂ label font size (and add a little clearance above the bulbs) so the primary captions dominate over secondary text at inline scale.
Keep the stopcock handle geometry identical across panels (indicate open/closed via the plug/bore only) so the hardware matches the source in all three snapshots.
